newsitem.title: MEXICO: GModelo 1996 results buoyed by exports.
newsitem.headline: GModelo 1996 results buoyed by exports.

text.p: A strong rise in 1996 profits for Mexican beer giant Grupo Modelo reflected a vibrant export performance but some back-sliding in the domestic market, analysts said.

"Modelo's export business was outstanding and solidified the firm's position as Mexico's leading exporter. Exports account for 13.6 percent of total volumes," said Bear Stearns analysts Carlos Laboy and Hector Tassinari in a report.

"However, we continued to observe a change in momentum on the domestic side of the business," it added, noting that market share, which Modelo had increased for at least 15 straight years, has been stagnant for two consecutive years.
Modelo reported that domestic volumes grew by 6.5 percent in 1996 to 23.67 million hectoliters, while export volumes were up 28.8 percent to 3.71 million hectoliters. A hectoliter is 100 liters.

But the volumes were offset in revenue terms by a domestic beer price decline estimated around four percent, which pushed down income in the domestic market by 7.3 percent. Export revenues, meanwhile, rose 7.2 percent over 1995.
Modelo raised prices on its various brands between 20 and 25 percent in March 1996, but Mexican inflation for the year rose 27.7 percent.

Notwithstanding the real price declines, Modelo reported a net profit of 1.249 billion pesos versus 1.068 billion pesos in 1995, which translated as earnings per share of 1.54 pesos versus 1.31 pesos.

"Their performance was strong in light of the real price reductions," said Greg Rianhard, beverage analyst at Los Angeles-based D.A. Campbell. "Despite sales declines, operating income increased by nearly four percent."
Analysts noted that Modelo's operating margins grew to 19.4 percent from 17.8 percent in 1995, partly due to lower grain prices and also because of improved efficiency.
Rianhard expected volume growth domestically of 4-5 percent in 1997, as well as export growth of 18 percent, though he noted that both forecasts were conservative.

Rianhard said he expects Modelo to introduce a 17 percent or more nominal price hike around March. The Mexican government is targeting inflation this year of 15 percent, but most economists expect it to be around 18 percent.
In a news release, Modelo said its fastest-growing export brands were Corona Light, Corona Extra and Pacifico, up 42.7 percent, 29.0 percent and 27.9 percent, respectively.

"The outstanding export performance was due to the increasing market penetration in states within the U.S. that had previously been ignored by the group, coupled with high growth in the group's new export markets in Europe and Asia," said Thomas Mobille, analyst at Flemings Research in Brazil.

Though he has the brewer as a long-term buy, Mobille noted that the company's present valuations fully account for a strong position against its rival Femsa, its fast-growing export volumes and its net cash position.

Other analysts also expressed some reserve. Bear Stearns said it remained concerned that the auditors of Modelo's partner Anheuser-Busch continued to disagree with Modelo on material issues affecting Modelo's value.

Its analysts also expected lower operating profit margins of 18.8 percent in 1997 as the new Zacatecas plant moves through its early ramp-up phase, and because Modelo continues with its push into northern Mexico, where distribution is more expensive.

Raul Romero of BBV-Probursa termed the Modelo report a "bad" one, saying margins declined considerably compared with the third quarter. Other analysts, however, said that may have been the result of seasonal factors. Romero kept a "hold" recomendation on Modelo.
